curriculum.lesson_evidence: Kindness is thinking about other people's needs and acting to help. Acts of kindness in a community include helping a neighbour, welcoming a newcomer, thanking workers, tidying shared spaces and sharing time or food with people in need. Kind actions work best when they are safe, respect the other person's wishes and do not expect anything back. Small acts can make a big difference.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Write one safe act of kindness for a lonely neighbour and one way to ask first so you respect their wishes.

FEEDBACK
Act: draw a card and have an adult deliver it. Asking: 'Would you like a card, or a visit, from me?' Respecting wishes makes the kindness welcome, and an adult keeps it safe.

WATCH FOR
Thinking kindness has to cost money or be big. Words, time and small actions are kind too.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Plan a one-week kindness project for your community with five actions (home, school, neighbourhood). For each, name who it helps, how it is safe and who would help you. Do at least two and record how people responded.

Write a short reflection naming one choice you changed and why. Any movement is optional, adult-supervised and can be done in a gentler way or described instead.

WORKED MODEL

teach_steps.explain:
Kindness is thinking about other people's needs and acting to help. Acts of kindness in a community include helping a neighbour, welcoming a newcomer, thanking workers, tidying shared spaces and sharing time or food with people in need. Kind actions work best when they are safe, respect the other person's wishes and do not expect anything back. Small acts can make a big difference.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make safe, healthy and respectful choices using clear cues and reasons, rather than guessing or copying others. Every choice keeps bodies safe and includes everyone.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the cues, rules or choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For any movement, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby, move at your own comfortable level and stop if anything hurts or feels unsafe. You may always choose a gentler version or only describe the movement. One deliberate, reasoned change is more useful than a longer answer.
